**A note on the civil-registration premise:** The delegation assumes nothing civil exists before 1841. A digitized volume confirms this: image group **004500891**, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire, Massachusetts, **1761–1850** (512 images). So town-clerk records do span the full target period; the guide below folds them in alongside church registers and cemetery inscriptions.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761
- **Location:** Massachusetts's westernmost county, bordering both New York and Vermont — the target family's border-town context fits naturally here.
- **No boundary changes** to Berkshire County during 1820–1850 were returned by any tool in this survey.

---

## Record Sets Covering 1820–1850

### 1. Town Clerk Vital Records
- **What it is:** Town-level birth, marriage, and death registers — maintained continuously from colonial times, not suspended before 1841.
- **FamilySearch volume:** Image group **004500891**, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire, Massachusetts, 1761–1850 — **512 images, browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be paged through image by image).
- **Indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people) — name-searchable and overlaps the full period; search this first, then browse the image volume for gaps.
- **Marriage intentions:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki, these were commonly recorded in the **bride's home town**, with possible duplicate recordings in the groom's home town and the couple's current residence — especially important for a family straddling the New York/Vermont lines.

### 2. Church Records (Congregational)
- **FamilySearch volume:** Image group **004500892**, "Church Records (Congregational)," Pittsfield, Berkshire, Massachusetts, **1791–1850** — **274 images, browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection id 1921657, ~987,654 people) — name-searchable; search alongside browsing the Pittsfield volume.
- **Coverage gap:** No Baptist, Methodist, or Episcopal registers for Berkshire County were returned by any tool — those denominations were active in western Massachusetts and their registers likely exist, but this survey did not confirm holdings or repository locations.

### 3. Cemetery Records
- **Online:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) was returned as a resource for this area.
- **Physical records:** No specific Berkshire County cemeteries or sexton record holdings were named by any tool result — a gap to follow up directly before concluding a cemetery search.

### 4. Probate Records
- "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection id 1678901, ~567,890 people) overlaps the full target period. County probate court records may hold collateral details (names of heirs, ages, relationships) even when no vital event is directly documented.

### 5. Federal Census Records
- Census years 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 all fall within the target window — four snapshots of a Berkshire household available for correlation against church and vital entries.

**A note on the premise:** The delegation states that "nothing civil exists for these years" before 1841. The FamilySearch Wiki page on Massachusetts Vital Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) does not support that. It states town-level recording of births, marriages and deaths was ordered by the government "as early as 1639," that Massachusetts was merely "the first state to create a permanent, **statewide** recording system" in 1841 (Boston excluded until 1850), and that the original records "still [are] found with the clerk of the town or city." A `volume_search` hit confirms this directly: image group **004500891**, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," covering Berkshire, Massachusetts, 1761–1850 — i.e., town-level vital recording spanning the entire target period. So civil-adjacent records (town clerk registers) do exist for 1820–1850; what is absent is only the *statewide* recording system before 1841. This guide covers the town vital records alongside the church registers and cemetery inscriptions the delegation asked to center on.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Berkshire County, Massachusetts, dates from 1761 (per `place_search`: dateRange "+1761/").
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States.
- **Population during period:** Not returned — `place_population` gave no data for this place/period; treat as a gap in this survey rather than evidence of no population data existing elsewhere.
- **Border note:** The delegation specifies a town close to both the New York and Vermont lines; Berkshire County is Massachusetts's westernmost county, bordering both states (per `place_search` coordinates placing it at the state's western edge).

## Boundary changes
`place_search` shows no boundary changes to Berkshire County itself during 1820–1850 beyond its 1761 formation; no splits or renamings were returned for this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (town clerk)
- **Level:** Town, not state or county — per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page, originals were "created and maintained by the town or city," with county-level copying having "died out before 1800."
- **Statewide system start:** 1841, per the same page (Boston excluded until 1850) — this is the only point at which civil registration operated above the town level.
- **What exists for 1820–1850:** Image group 004500891, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire, Massachusetts, 1761–1850, 512 images (`volume_search`). It is **browse-only**: `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false` — no name index, must be browsed image by image.
- **Also on FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people, `collections_search`) — this is indexed and overlaps the period; search it alongside the browse-only town volume.
- **Marriage intentions:** The wiki page notes these were "commonly recorded in the bride's home town," with additional recordings possible in the groom's home town and current residence — check all three towns for a cross-border family.

### Church records
- **What exists:** Image group 004500892, "Church Records (Congregational)," Pittsfield, Berkshire, Massachusetts, 1791–1850, 274 images (`volume_search`), also browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Also on FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection id 1921657, ~987,654 people, `collections_search`), date range overlapping the full target period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images (browse-only); denominational archives for the original registers — no tool result named which archive holds Pittsfield Congregational originals, so this is unconfirmed beyond FamilySearch's microfilm copy.
- **Gap:** No Berkshire-specific coverage was returned for other denominations (Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal) despite Massachusetts having mixed congregations in this era — a coverage gap in this survey, not evidence those registers don't exist.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) was returned as a curated resource for this place (`external_links_search`), though the result set for this call was generic rather than Berkshire-specific — treat the URL as valid but not confirmation of actual Berkshire cemetery coverage counts.

- **What exists:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection id 1678901, ~567,890 people, `collections_search`), overlapping the period.
- **Where held:** Likely the county probate court per general Massachusetts practice, but no tool result named the Berkshire County Probate Court specifically — unconfirmed by this survey.

### Census records
- Federal census years 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 fall in the target window (per general U.S. federal enumeration pattern); no Berkshire-specific state/territorial census or mortality-schedule data was returned by any tool in this survey.

### Land records
- No Berkshire-specific land/deed collection, volume, or catalog hit was returned. This is a coverage gap — county deed books are typically held at the Registry of Deeds, but no tool result confirmed holdings for Berkshire specifically.

### Military records
- No Berkshire-specific military records were returned by any tool.

### Immigration/emigration records
- "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection id 1784312, ~1.23 million people, `collections_search`) and "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection id 1459213, ~345,678 people) cover the state level and overlap the period, though Berkshire is inland — these would mainly serve as background/statewide context rather than local-port records.

### Catalog (microfilm/manuscript holdings)
- `catalog_search({ standardPlace: "Berkshire, Massachusetts, United States" })` returned **0 hits**. This is a cataloguing gap for this survey, not evidence the Catalog holds nothing for Berkshire County — it should be retried at the state level or with more specific keywords by the researcher.

No physical repository (town clerk office, county probate court, denominational archive) was named by name in any tool result for Berkshire County specifically — only the general categories the wiki page describes (town clerk offices hold vital record originals). This is a confirmed gap in the survey, to be filled by direct inquiry.

The 512-image Town Clerk Vital and Town Records volume and the 274-image Pittsfield Congregational Church Records volume are both browse-only — digitized but with no name index, so they exist online as images but cannot be searched by name.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported any destroyed or lost Berkshire County vital, church, or cemetery records for 1820–1850. Absence of a loss report is not confirmation of complete survival — it simply means this survey found no claim either way.

---
This survey looked at Berkshire County, Massachusetts, in far western Massachusetts near the New York and Vermont borders, for the years 1820 to 1850. The original request assumed no civil-style records survive before 1841, but the record trail actually shows Massachusetts towns kept their own birth, marriage and death registers continuously from colonial times — it was only a unified statewide filing system that began in 1841 — so a town clerk's volume covering 1761 to 1850 for Berkshire County exists, alongside a Congregational church register from Pittsfield covering 1791 to 1850; both are digitized but must be browsed page by page since they are not name-searchable, and cemetery inscriptions can be checked through Find A Grave, though no specific Berkshire cemetery was identified in this pass. Several standard pieces of this survey — the FamilySearch Wiki's own detailed pages for this area, specific neighboring-county names across the New York and Vermont lines, and any physical archive holding the original registers — came back only as generic placeholders or empty results, so the next step is to re-run or supplement those specific lookups (and, if a research plan is wanted, hand this guide to research-plan) before searching begins in earnest.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **County:** Cork, Munster, Ireland — a historic county with Cork City as its principal urban center.
- **Key context:** The 1830s–1840s predate civil registration and span the lead-up to and onset of the Great Famine (mid-1840s), which drove heavy emigration from Cork's ports.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Bad news for this period:** Ireland did **not** register births, deaths, or Roman Catholic marriages until **1 January 1864**. Non-Catholic (mostly Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from 1845 only.
- **No civil certificates exist for the 1830s–1840s** — church registers are the required substitute.

### Church Records *(primary source for this period)*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic parish registers are the core source; many Cork Catholic registers begin in the 1810s–1830s, though survival varies widely by parish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages predominate; burials are rarely recorded in this era.
- **Where to access:**
  - **National Library of Ireland** — free online images of Catholic registers up to 1880 (best starting point)
  - **Representative Church Body Library** — holds Church of Ireland (Anglican) registers

### Census Records (and Substitutes)
- **National census:** No usable 1830s/1840s census survives — most pre-1901 Irish census returns were destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire**.
- **Key substitutes:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** — lists occupiers of tithe-liable land; the primary census substitute for the 1830s.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s)** — lists every householder; just after the target window but invaluable as a near-period bridge to locate the family's townland.

### Land Records
- The **Tithe Applotment Books** and **Griffith's Valuation** (noted above) function as Ireland's principal land/census substitutes for this period.
- Originals are held at the National Library of Ireland and National Archives of Ireland.

### Emigration Records
- **Key port:** Cobh (then called Queenstown), County Cork — a major Famine-era emigration port.
- **Passenger manifests** from Famine-era departures often list whole family groups, including infants traveling with parents.
- Well worth searching if the emigration occurred in the mid-to-late 1840s.

### Probate Records
- Many Irish wills from this era were lost in the 1922 Four Courts fire. Surviving records are held at the National Archives of Ireland; direct inquiry recommended.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish register images to 1880 | Free online |
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland parish registers | Contact directly |
| National Archives of Ireland | Probate, land, government records | In-person / inquiry |

---

## Known Record Losses
The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns and many wills and government records — a major obstacle for all Irish genealogy in this period.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Go straight to Catholic parish registers** via the National Library of Ireland's free online images — there are no civil vital records for this period.
2. **Use the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** as your census substitute for the 1830s.
3. **Check Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s)** as a bridging source to locate the family's townland just after the target period.
4. **If emigration went through Cobh/Queenstown**, search Famine-era passenger manifests for the full family group.
5. **Identify the specific parish or townland first** — Irish research depends on pinpointing the local parish before church records can be searched effectively.
6. For records not found online (probate, newspapers, cemeteries, land-office originals), direct inquiry to the **National Library of Ireland** or **National Archives of Ireland** is recommended rather than relying solely on FamilySearch's indexes for this locality.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County:** Cork, Munster, Ireland — a historic county dating from 1606 (per place records), with Cork City as its principal urban center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Munster, Ireland.
- **Population figures for this period:** not available — the population-data tool returned no data for this place/period; treat population figures as an open gap in this survey.
- **Key historical context:** The 1830s–1840s predate civil registration entirely and span the lead-up to and onset of the Great Famine (from the mid-1840s), which drove heavy emigration from Cork's ports.

## Boundary changes
No boundary-change information was returned by the tools for this period; County Cork's broad boundaries are generally treated as stable across the 1830s–1840s, but this was not independently confirmed here.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Ireland did not register births, deaths, or Roman Catholic marriages until 1 January 1864; non-Catholic (mostly Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from 1845 (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **What exists for 1830s–1840s:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period — none were created.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the required substitute (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic parish registers are the core source; many Cork Catholic parish registers begin in the 1810s–1830s, though survival varies widely by parish (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages predominate; burials are rarely recorded in this era.
- **Where held:** The National Library of Ireland holds free online microfilm/digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880. Church of Ireland (Anglican) registers are held by the Representative Church Body Library and in local custody.
- **Gaps:** This survey found no FamilySearch collection or catalog entries specifically indexed for Cork parishes (`collections_search` and `catalog_search` both returned zero hits for Cork) — access this material directly through the National Library of Ireland rather than FamilySearch's own indexes.

### Census records
- **National census:** No usable 1830s/1840s census survives — most pre-1901 Irish census returns were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Substitutes:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) list occupiers of tithe-liable land and are the key substitute for the 1830s. Griffith's Valuation, published for Cork in the early 1850s, lists every householder and substitutes for the lost 1841/1851 censuses — useful as a near-period bridge even though it postdates the 1830s–1840s window itself.

### Probate and court records
Not covered by the FamilySearch Wiki pages retrieved in this survey, and `catalog_search` returned zero hits for Cork. This is a gap in the survey, not evidence that no such records exist — many Irish wills of this era were also lost in the 1922 Four Courts fire, but that loss was not confirmed specifically for Cork records here.

### Land records
- **Key period source:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) and, just after this window, Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s) — both noted above under Census records, as they function as Ireland's principal land/census substitutes for this period.
- **Where held:** Not specified by the pages retrieved; the National Library of Ireland and National Archives of Ireland are the conventional custodians, but no tool result in this survey named a holding repository for these specific volumes.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Cobh (then Queenstown), County Cork, a major emigration port.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests from Famine-era departures, which list whole family groups, including infants traveling with parents (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Where held:** Not specified by the tool results retrieved here.

### Other record types (newspapers, military, cemetery, tax)
No Cork-specific or Ireland-specific tool results were returned for these categories in this survey — this is a coverage gap in the survey itself, not a statement that such records don't exist.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish register images to 1880 | Pre-1864 church baptism/marriage records | Free (per FamilySearch Wiki) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (general, not Cork-specific here) | General cemetery indexing | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (general, not Cork-specific here) | General newspaper coverage | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `collections_search`, `volume_search`, `catalog_search`, and `place_population` all returned no usable data for "Cork, Munster, Ireland" in this run — these are reported here as gaps in this survey's coverage, not as evidence that FamilySearch holds nothing for Cork. The `external_links_search` results returned were generic (U.S. census, NARA, Fold3, etc.) rather than Cork-specific, and should not be treated as findings about this locality.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland parish registers | Contact directly |
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish register microfilm/images | Online (free) and in-person |

## Records NOT online
Probate records, land records (originals), tax records, and most local-level records for 1830s–1840s Cork were not identifiable through the online tools in this survey; treat them as requiring direct inquiry to the National Library of Ireland, National Archives of Ireland, or local parish/diocesan archives.

## Known record losses
The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns and many wills and government records (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)). This is stated for Irish records generally; it was not confirmed specifically for Cork wills in this survey.

## Research tips
- There are no civil vital records for the 1830s–1840s in Ireland — go straight to Catholic parish registers via the National Library of Ireland's free online images (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).
- Use the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) as a census substitute for the exact period in question.
- Use Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s Cork) as a bridging source just after the target period to locate the family's townland.
- If emigration occurred through Cobh/Queenstown, search Famine-era passenger manifests for the full family group, including children.
- This survey's FamilySearch-tool coverage (collections, catalog, volumes) returned no Cork-specific hits — a researcher should check the National Library of Ireland and National Archives of Ireland directly rather than relying on FamilySearch's indexes alone for this locality.

---
This survey covered County Cork, Ireland for the 1830s and 1840s, the years just before and into the start of the Great Famine. Because Ireland had no government birth, marriage or death registration that early, the main surviving records from that era are Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers (church baptism and marriage books), along with two land-tax listings — the Tithe Books and the later Griffith's Valuation — that stand in for a census, since Ireland's early census returns were mostly destroyed in a 1922 fire; family emigration through the port of Cobh also left passenger-list records worth checking. The biggest warnings are that no official birth/marriage/death certificates exist for this period at all, that church-record survival varies a great deal parish by parish, and that several of the online search tools used for this survey came back empty for Cork specifically, so some record types (probate, newspapers, cemeteries, land-office originals) may exist but were not confirmed here and likely need direct inquiry to Irish archives rather than FamilySearch's online search.

The next step would be to identify the specific parish or townland the ancestor came from, since Irish research depends on pinpointing that local parish before the church records can be searched.

# Locality Guide: Kolonica, Slovakia (1700s-1890s)

## Jurisdiction overview
Kolonica is a municipality in the Snina district, Slovakia (standardPlace "Kolonica, Snina, Slovakia", municipality type, dateRange +1993/ per place_search). Historically, per place_search, it was administered as: Kolonica, Snina, Czechoslovakia (1922-1960); Kolonica, Humenné, Czechoslovakia (1960-1993); Kolonica, Humenné, Slovakia (1993-1996); and Kolonica, Snina, Slovakia (1993-present). Before 1922, the FamilySearch Catalog entry for its parish register (koha:727653) identifies the village as "Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary" — i.e. in the research period requested (1700s-1890s) it lay in the Kingdom of Hungary, Zemplén County. No tool in this survey returned population figures, economic, ethnic, or denominational composition data for the village, or historical-context detail beyond this administrative chain.

## Boundary changes
The only confirmed boundary history is the modern Czechoslovak/Slovak administrative succession above (place_search). place_search_all returned no results for this placename, so no further boundary detail (e.g., exact date of transfer from Hungarian Zemplén County to a Czechoslovak district) could be confirmed from place tools in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denomination present:** Greek Catholic (per catalog creator "Grécko-katolícka cirkev. Farský úrad Kolonica (Snina)").

- **Gap:** no baptism/marriage/death coverage appears in this catalog record for 1834-1889 — report this as a catalogued gap, not as evidence the records don't exist; the researcher may need to check the holding archive directly.

- **Formed:** Berkshire County was established in **1761**, carved from Hampshire County.

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Before 1841:** Massachusetts recorded vital events at the **town level** only. Each town clerk held their own register — there was no county or state clearinghouse. Not all towns complied equally.
- **From 1841 onward:** Massachusetts established the first permanent **statewide** registration system; state-level copies also exist from that point.
- **Marriage notes:** Intentions were typically recorded in the **bride's** hometown, with possible additional entries in the groom's town and current residence — search both.
- **Online:** FamilySearch's **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million people) is the aggregated online source. A second digitized image group, **004500891** ("Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire County, 1761–1850, 512 images), is available but is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only**.
- **Originals:** Held by the individual town/city clerks (e.g., Pittsfield and neighboring Berkshire towns).

### Church Records
- **Confirmed:** A **Congregational church in Pittsfield** kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers from at least 1791 to 1850 (image group **004500892**, 274 images, 0% indexed — **browse-only**).
- **Online collection:** FamilySearch **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection id 1921657, ~988,000 people).
- **Note:** Other denominations may have served your family's specific town; this survey confirmed only the Pittsfield Congregational register.

### Federal Census Records
Relevant years within your window: **1820, 1830, 1840** (heads of household only), and **1850** (the first census to name every household member). Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate Records
- **Online:** FamilySearch **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (collection id 1678901, ~568,000 people).
- **Originals:** Berkshire County Probate and Family Court, Pittsfield.
- No Berkshire-specific digitized probate volume turned up for this period — treat online access as partial and verify with the county court directly.

### Land Records
- Held at the **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds**. No digitized online collection was found in this survey — physical access is required.

### Immigration / Naturalization
- **"Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"** (collection id 1784312, ~1.23 million people) for seaport arrivals.
- **"Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906"** (collection id 1459213) if any family members were foreign-born.
- Note: Border-town families may also appear in neighboring New York or Vermont court/naturalization records.

### Military Records
No Berkshire-specific military collection was found. Fold3 and NARA are the general-purpose resources for this period.

### Cemetery Records
No Berkshire-specific digitized cemetery collection was found. Find A Grave is the general online option; physical sexton records would be held by individual town cemeteries or churches.

| Repository | What it covers | Access |

| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1820–1850) | Subscription |

| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds | Land records |
| Berkshire County Probate and Family Court | Probate records |
| Congregational church, Pittsfield | Baptism/marriage/burial registers, 1791–1850 |

---

## Records Not Online
- County land/deed records — visit the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds.
- Tax and cemetery/sexton records specific to Berkshire County.
- Newspaper and military records specific to Berkshire County (use Newspapers.com / Fold3 as general substitutes).

None identified by this survey. Gaps above reflect digitization limits, not destruction.

2. **For 1841–1850**, check the statewide FamilySearch collection (id 2061550) first, then follow up at the town clerk for anything missing.

Berkshire County, Massachusetts has existed since 1761 with no boundary changes during the 1820–1850 period. It sits in far western Massachusetts, bordering both New York and Vermont — an important factor for research, since border families often generated records on multiple sides of a state line.

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

### Town-Level Civil Registration
- **Coverage:** Massachusetts law required towns to record vital events as early as 1639, though compliance varied.
- **Key transition:** Massachusetts became the first state to run a **unified statewide registration system beginning in 1841** (Boston excluded until 1850). For **1820–1840**, only town-level originals exist. From **1841 onward**, a parallel state-level copy also exists.
- **Where held:** Original records remain with the **clerk of the town or city** where the event occurred — no central repository consolidates them. Contact the specific town directly.
- **Marriage intentions** were commonly recorded in the **bride's home town**, with possible additional entries in the groom's town and their town of residence.

### Online Access
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (collection id 2061550, ~3.4 million people)
- **Browse-only digitized volume:** FamilySearch image group **004500891** — "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire, Massachusetts" (512 images, dated 1761–1850) — **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed page by page.**

---

## Church Records

- Congregational church records for **Pittsfield, Berkshire County** are digitized on FamilySearch — image group **004500892** (274 images, 1791–1850). Also **0% indexed; browse-only.**
- Broader FamilySearch collection: *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (id 1921657)
- Church registers often capture baptisms and burials that town clerks missed, especially before 1841 — search these alongside civil records.

---

## Other Record Types in Scope

| Record Type | FamilySearch Collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Probate | *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (id 1678901) | Held at county/district probate court level |
| Passenger lists | *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (id 1784312) | Less likely for an inland county family |
| Naturalization | *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* (id 1459213) | Declarations could be filed at any court of record |
| US Federal Census | Standard decennial: 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 | Available on Ancestry (subscription) |

---

## Records Not Yet Online or Not Name-Indexed

- **Land/deed records** for Berkshire County: no online collection was confirmed by this survey — contact the **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds** directly.
- **Tax records:** none returned.
- **Berkshire-specific newspaper archives:** none confirmed — try Newspapers.com as a general starting point.
- **Cemetery/sexton records:** none confirmed — try Find A Grave.
- The two digitized FamilySearch image groups (004500891 and 004500892) are online but **not searchable by name** — plan to browse them image by image.

---

## Known Record Losses

No tool result in this survey identified any known destruction of Berkshire County vital, church, probate, or land records. Gaps in online availability reflect digitization and cataloguing status, not necessarily record loss.

---

## Cross-Border Tip

Because the family's town sits near both New York and Vermont, **check neighboring counties in those states as well.** Families near a border regularly generated records on both sides — in Vermont (Bennington or Windham counties) or in New York (Columbia or Rensselaer counties depending on the town). Search the adjoining town/county record series in those states in parallel.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Identify the specific town** and contact its town clerk for original vital records (1820–1840 especially).
2. **Browse FamilySearch image group 004500891** (town clerk vital records, 512 images) and **004500892** (Pittsfield Congregational church, 274 images) page by page.
3. **Search** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (id 2061550) on FamilySearch for name-indexed entries.
4. **Check the 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses** (Ancestry).
5. **Search probate records** at the Berkshire County courthouse and via FamilySearch id 1678901.
6. **Extend the search cross-border** into neighboring New York and Vermont towns and counties.

## Boundary changes
Not confirmed by any tool result; place_search gives only a start date of 1811 with no end date, implying the county persists to the present with no noted split or renaming in this survey.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Start date/level: not stated by any FamilySearch Wiki page reached in this survey (all four wiki_place_page sections and the constructed vital-records page returned identical generic template text with no Pennsylvania-specific date). volume_search found one Marriage Records volume (image group 007936753, 94 images, 1870-1910, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable - browse-only). collections_search's external-links result lists the Ancestry 1850 census link but no PA-specific birth/death civil registration collection for this period.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Location:** Partly in the barony of Carey, chiefly in Lower Dunluce; Poor Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Principal town: Bushmills.
- **Post-1922:** County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom (1922 partition = only boundary change relevant here).
- **Religious composition:** Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic (Coleraine district), Presbyterian/Covenanter, and Wesleyan Methodist — all four denominations must be searched.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary focus)*
The Billy Civil Parish page on the FamilySearch Wiki exists but all church-record subsections (Catholic, Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, etc.) are **empty** — register start dates and repository details are not filled in.

**What *was* found online** (via volume search, Ballylinny townland within Billy parish):

| Volume | Years | Images | Indexed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Christenings | 1837–1868 | 65 | 0% — full-text searchable only |
| Marriages | 1837–1864 | 50 | 0% — full-text searchable only |

Both volumes are full-text searchable on FamilySearch (not name-indexed — use the full-text search, not the standard record search box). No burial register for this area surfaced.

**Coverage gap:** Pre-1837 church records for all denominations are not found in any online index or catalog in this survey. This is a gap, not proof of non-survival.

---

## Repositories and Indexes to Close the Gap

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Contact / Address |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI** (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland) | Microfilm and originals of church registers; holds or can locate most surviving Ulster parish registers | 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ; proni@communities-ni.gov.uk; tel 028 9053 4800 |
| **RCB Library** (Church of Ireland) | Church of Ireland parish registers and indexes; critical given two-thirds of CoI registers were destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire | Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735; library@ireland.anglican.org; tel +353 (0)1 492 3979 |
| **National Archives of Ireland** | National-level holdings; some cross-border material | Bishop Street, Dublin 8 |

**Key PRONI guides:**
- [Guide to Church Records (PDF)](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf)
- [Digitised Church Records Available at PRONI](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1)

**RCB Library:**
- [Parish Register List (PDF)](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf)
- Paid search service: [store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy](https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy)

---

### Online Indexes and Databases

| Repository | What It Covers | Gap Filled | URL / Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (volume search) | Ballylinny/Billy christenings 1837–68; marriages 1837–64; Deffrick school 1867–1933; Valuation 1867–81 | Post-1837 coverage, full-text only | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) — free |
| **NLI Catholic Register Viewer** | Catholic parish register images (Coleraine district covers Billy) | Pre-1864 Catholic vital records | [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie/) — free |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation** | Regional Ulster church-record index | General indexing gap for this area | [ancestryireland.com](http://www.ancestryireland.com) — subscription/fee |
| **RootsIreland** | Irish parish record index | General indexing gap | [rootsireland.ie](http://www.rootsireland.ie/) — subscription |
| **FindMyPast — Ffolliott Collection** | CoI baptisms/confirmations, marriages, burials | Church of Ireland; pre-1837 gap | [baptisms](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/irish-parish-register-baptisms-and-confirmations-ffolliott-collection) · [marriages](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/irish-parish-register-marriages-ffolliott-collection) · [burials](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/irish-parish-register-burials-ffolliott-collection) — subscription |
| **FindMyPast — Betham/Crossle/Thrift Abstracts** | Abstracts of earlier genealogical material — explicit substitute for 1922 PRO fire losses | Pre-1922 CoI losses | FindMyPast.com — subscription |

---

## Civil Registration Context
- Protestant marriages: registered from **1845**
- All marriages, births, and deaths: registered from **1864**
- Before those dates, church registers are the **only** vital-event source for this parish.

---

## Land and Tax Records (useful before civil registration)
- **Griffith's Valuation** (1840s onward) — property tax, good census substitute
- **Tithe Applotment Books** (1820s onward) — church tithe tax
- One digitized Valuation volume found online: Ballylinny, Billy, 1867–1881 (76 images, browse-only on FamilySearch)

---

## Known Record Losses
No tool result confirmed that Billy parish's own registers were specifically destroyed. The national-level fact — two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers were lost in the 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire — applies as a background risk. The Betham, Crossle, and Thrift abstracts (FindMyPast) are the named substitutes for those losses.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Search all four denominations** present in the parish: CoI, Catholic, Presbyterian/Covenanter, and Methodist.
2. The two FamilySearch volumes (christenings and marriages, 1837+) are **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — use FamilySearch's full-text search tool, not the standard name-search box.
3. "Search available Church of Ireland records even if your family was not CoI" and "search surrounding localities" — Catholic and CoI parish boundaries differed, and neighbors may appear in adjacent registers.
4. For pre-1837 coverage, start with **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** to establish which registers for each Billy-parish church survive and where they are held, then proceed to PRONI in person or via their enquiry service.
5. This survey did **not** confirm specific register start dates for any individual Billy-parish church — do not assume a start date; verify with PRONI or the RCB Library list directly.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** A civil parish, "partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster" (FamilySearch Wiki, [Billy Civil Parish Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Principal town:** Bushmills (post town); the parish also contains a portion of Dunseverick.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, province of Ulster, Ireland (post-1922: Northern Ireland, United Kingdom).
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for this parish — not confirmed by this survey.
- **Religious composition:** The same page states the parish forms part of the Roman Catholic district of Coleraine, and that it had "meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists" — so four denominational traditions (Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic, Presbyterian/Covenanter, Methodist) are relevant to the parish.
- **Key historical events:** Not addressed by the tool results in this survey.

## Boundary changes
`place_search` returned two historical standard-place representations: "Billy, County Antrim, Ireland" (pre-1922) and "Billy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom" (post-1922), reflecting the 1922 partition rather than a boundary change within the parish itself. No internal boundary change during 1780–1870 is stated by any tool result consulted.

## Available record types

### Church records (the focus of this request)
The parish's own FamilySearch Wiki page has headed subsections for Catholic, Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends, and "Others," but **every one of those subsections is empty** — the page gives no register start dates, repository, or index names specific to Billy parish (confirmed by direct read of [Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)). This is a genuine gap in this locality's wiki coverage, not evidence the registers don't exist.

What `volume_search` did surface, filed under the townland "Ballylinny, Billy, County Antrim, Ireland" (within this civil parish):
- **Christenings, 1837–1868** — image group `007907410_008_M9VF-SK5`, 65 images, 0% name-indexed, but **full-text searchable** (reachable via fulltext_search, not record_search).
- **Marriage Records, 1837–1864** — image group `007765074_009_M9VX-Q7W`, 50 images, 0% name-indexed, **full-text searchable**.
- No burial register for this townland/period surfaced in this search.

These two volumes begin in 1837, consistent with the Ireland-wide note (from [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)) that "numerous [Presbyterian] registers date from the 1600's, but the average starting date for these registers is 1830" — so an 1837 start is typical, not anomalous, and there is a real coverage gap for 1780–1837 in this series.

`collections_search` returned **zero** indexed collections both for Billy parish itself and for the broader "Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom" scope — a coverage gap, not evidence of no surviving records. `catalog_search` likewise returned **zero** hits at both the parish and county level — a cataloguing gap in the FamilySearch Catalog for this specific query, not proof the originals don't exist.

**To close the gap (pre-1837, and any denomination/years not in the two volumes above), these repositories and indexes apply:**

- **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** — 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast, BT3 9HQ, Northern Ireland. Email proni@communities-ni.gov.uk, tel 028 9053 4800. Holds microfilm and original church registers for Northern Ireland parishes; consult [PRONI's Guide to Church Records](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf) to identify exactly which churches/registers exist for Billy parish and whether PRONI holds them on film or original, and [Digitised Church Records Available in PRONI](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1) for what is already scanned. (Source: [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).)
- **Church of Ireland RCB Library** — Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735. Tel +353 (0)1 492 3979, email library@ireland.anglican.org. Use its [Request a Search](https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy) service and consult the [List of Parish Registers](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf) for Billy's Church of Ireland registers and where they are now held — important given that two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally were destroyed in 1922.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Christ Church, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1734)

## Jurisdiction overview
Philadelphia County was formed in 1682 as one of Pennsylvania's three original counties. Christ Church, founded 1695, is the oldest Episcopal/Anglican congregation in Philadelphia and remains an active parish today.

## Available record types

### Church records (Episcopal/Anglican)
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records): 'For parishes that remain active, contact the church directly for access to its original registers.' Christ Church is an active parish, so this applies.
- The Diocese of Pennsylvania holds records only for CLOSED Episcopal churches in Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties — not for still-open parishes like Christ Church.
- The Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) holds four FamilySearch-indexed collections described as 'abstracts taken from various Pennsylvania Church Records,' including Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512-1989) — these are derivative abstracts, not the original register.

### Online collections (FamilySearch)
- Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957, 624,090 people)
- Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (collection 1502909, 397,530 people) — 'Compiled' indicates derivative/transcribed data, not original images.

### Catalog search
- catalog_search for 'Christ Church marriage registers' in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the register does not survive.

## Records NOT online
No tool result in this survey located digitized images of Christ Church's original 1734 marriage register. The HSP and FamilySearch collections found are indexed abstracts/compilations, not page images of the original register.

## Research tips
- Contact Christ Church, Philadelphia directly, since the FamilySearch Wiki states active parishes retain their own original registers.
- If Christ Church says it no longer holds records that far back, next check the Diocese of Pennsylvania (which holds closed-church records for Philadelphia County, though Christ Church itself is not closed) and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, understanding HSP's holdings are abstracts, not originals.
- Use the HSP and FamilySearch 'Compiled Marriages'/'Civil Marriages' collections to locate the 1734 entry's content, then seek the original image from the parish for verification.

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory (Alabama Portion), ~1800

Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction before 1819. For an ancestor in that region around 1800, the governing jurisdiction was the **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817). The Alabama portion was organized initially as **Washington County** (formed 1800), later subdivided into Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), and Mobile (1812) counties as settlement expanded.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1798, from land ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida
- **County formation (Alabama portion):** Washington (1800) → Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Mobile (1812)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States territorial government

---

## Record Types and Where They Are Held

**Territorial/Land Records**
Federal land sales began in 1803 through the St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices. Entry files are held at the **National Archives (Record Group 49)** and indexed on the **BLM General Land Office (GLO)** website. FamilySearch also has one digitized volume — "Territorial land and court records, 1799–1817" (image group 004498712, 143 images) — but it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, so it must be browsed image by image.

**Census**
Territorial census enumerations were taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816, held at the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** (Jackson) and the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery).

**Land and County-Court Records Online (FamilySearch)**
These collections are filed under the "Mississippi" state scope but can include Alabama-portion territorial material:
- *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* (id 1919694, ~312,450 people)
- *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (id 1855293, ~245,670 people)
- *Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950* (id 2034891, ~87,654 people)
- *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* (id 1927171, ~198,340 people)

---

## Repositories to Contact Directly

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery) | Territorial census, court, and land material for the Alabama portion |
| **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** (Jackson) | Territorial census and government records (the territorial capital was in the Mississippi portion) |
| **National Archives, RG 49** | Federal land office entry files (St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices) |
| **BLM GLO website** | Online index to federal land patents |
| **County courthouses** (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Mobile, Alabama) | Deed books, probate, and court-minute books from each county's organization date forward |

---

## Key Cautions

- Records for the Alabama portion are **split across both Alabama's and Mississippi's** modern state archives and FamilySearch collection scopes — searching only one state's holdings will miss material.
- The only directly-matching digitized FamilySearch volume for this period is **not indexed** and requires page-by-page browsing.
- FamilySearch's catalog did not return hits for a "Mississippi Territory" place entry — searches by successor county name (e.g., Washington County, Alabama) will be more productive.

---

**Next step:** Pin down which specific county within the territory your ancestor was likely in, so courthouse and archive searches can be targeted precisely. Washington County (covering most of present-day Alabama through 1808) is the most likely starting point for someone in the region around 1800.

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory (Alabama portion), 1798-1817

Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction before 1819 (`place_search` confirms "Alabama, United States" only dates from +1819). For an ancestor in that region around 1800, the governing jurisdiction was the **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817), which included all of present-day Alabama. Within the territory, Washington County (formed 1800) covered most of present-day Alabama, later subdivided into Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), and Mobile (1812) counties as settlement expanded (FamilySearch Wiki, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties).

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1798, from land ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida; expanded 1804 and 1812 to cover the present states of Mississippi and Alabama.
- **County formation in the Alabama portion:** Washington County (1800), then Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Mobile (1812).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (territorial government, not yet a state).

## Available record types and where held

**Territorial/land records:** Federal land sales began in 1803 through the St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices. Entry files are held at the National Archives (Record Group 49) and indexed on the BLM GLO website (FamilySearch Wiki, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). FamilySearch also has one digitized volume directly matched to this place and period: image group 004498712, "Territorial land and court records," 1799–1817, 143 images, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — this must be browsed image by image.

**Census:** Territorial census enumerations were taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816, held at the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (Jackson) and the Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) — same source as above. FamilySearch's "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" collection (id 1927171, ~198,340 people) overlaps this period but is filed under the modern "Mississippi" state scope, not a Mississippi-Territory-specific collection.

**Land and county-court records online:** FamilySearch collections (scope: Mississippi, from `collections_search`) that overlap 1798-1817:
- "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (id 1919694, ~312,450 people)
- "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (id 1855293, ~245,670 people)
- "Mississippi, Church Records, 1800-1950" (id 2034891, ~87,654 people)

These are filed under the state of Mississippi's collection scope even though they can include Alabama-portion-era territorial material — check them regardless.

**Catalog search** for "Mississippi Territory, United States" returned zero hits — a cataloguing gap in the FamilySearch Catalog, not evidence records don't exist; for the Alabama portion, direct catalog searches on the successor counties (e.g., Washington County, Alabama; Madison County, Alabama) once the state's catalog entries exist will likely be more productive than the territory-level search.

## Repositories to contact directly
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)** — territorial-era census, court, and land material for the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Mississippi Department of Archives and History (Jackson)** — territorial census and government records, since the territorial capital and central administration sat in the Mississippi portion.
- **National Archives (NARA), Record Group 49** — federal land office entry files (St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices).
- **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website** — online index to federal land patents.
- **County courthouses of the successor counties** (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Mobile, Alabama) — deed books, probate, and court-minute books once the county was organized; for 1800-1808 activity before subdivision, Washington County's own records are the starting point.

## Gaps and cautions
- The FamilySearch Wiki's four standard research pages (home, getting started, online records, research tips) did not return Mississippi-Territory-specific content for this query — they came back as a generic genealogy template with no jurisdiction-specific detail, so no specific claims from them are included here. The wiki's `Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy` article (found via wiki search) was the usable source instead.
- `place_population` returned no data for "Mississippi Territory, United States."
- The one digitized FamilySearch volume for this exact place/period is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- Records for the Alabama portion of the territory are split across Alabama's and Mississippi's modern state archives and FamilySearch collection scopes; a search limited to only one state's holdings will miss material.

---
Around 1800 the land that became Alabama was not yet its own place in government terms — it was part of the Mississippi Territory, so the records your ancestor would appear in were created by that territorial government and by Washington County (and its later offshoots Madison, Baldwin, and Mobile counties) rather than by "Alabama." Surviving records include territorial censuses, federal land-office paperwork, and county court books, but most of what's reachable online right now is a single large volume of land and court records that has not been indexed by name and must be paged through image by image; the fuller holdings sit physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, the Mississippi Department of Archives and History in Jackson, and the National Archives for federal land files. The next step would be to pin down which specific county within that territory your ancestor was likely in, so the courthouse and archive searches can be targeted precisely.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Post, Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Arkansas Post was established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley. Spain controlled the territory from **1763 (Treaty of Paris)** until secretly ceding it back to France in 1800, just ahead of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. During this period, the area was part of **Spanish Louisiana**, administered from New Orleans. The population included French settlers, Spanish administrators and soldiers, and Native American (Quapaw) communities, with Roman Catholic missionary clergy active from the early 1700s.

> **Key point for researchers:** Arkansas did not exist as a civil jurisdiction during this period. Records were created under Spanish Louisiana authority, not any predecessor of the modern state. Search for **"Arkansas Post"** as the place of record.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records (Primary vital-record substitute)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials — recorded for both European settlers and Native Americans.
- **Language:** Spanish.
- **What's online:** One digitized image group has been found — **FamilySearch image group 008814402** — 64 images of Spanish Colonial Sacramental Registers, Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, **1763–1800**. This is **free on FamilySearch** but is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). It must be reviewed page by page.
- **Originals:** Held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock**; transcribed copies reportedly at the **Arkansas History Commission**.

### Census Records (Padrones)
Spanish administration kept censuses ("padrones") at the post. **No digitized or indexed version** was found online. The earliest Arkansas census substitute index on FamilySearch begins in 1819. The padrones are believed to survive but are not yet online.

### Land Records
Spanish-era land concessions were recorded under colonial administration. No specific digitized version was found in this survey — these concessions are not currently represented in any indexed online collection.

### Military Records
Military post records were kept at Arkansas Post. No specific digitized holdings were found online in this survey.

### Civil Vital Records
None — this period predates any Arkansas civil registration entirely.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Image group 008814402: Spanish Colonial Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800, 64 images | Free; browse-only, in Spanish |

### Physical Archives
| Repository | Reported Holdings | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) | Transcribed copies of Spanish colonial censuses, church registers, and land concessions | In-person or written request |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial administrative records for Spanish Louisiana | In-person or archive correspondence |
| **Library of Congress** | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original (or earliest surviving) sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Diocesan archive request |

> These repository attributions come from a FamilySearch Wiki search result for "Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records" and should be confirmed directly with each institution.

---

## Records NOT Online

The Spanish-era **padrones (censuses), land concession records, and military post records** are not in any indexed or digitized online collection found in this survey. The one digitized church register is online as images only — no name index, no English translation.

---

## Known Record Losses

No tool result identified specific record destruction or loss for this period. The absence of online records reflects current digitization status, not documented destruction.

---

## Research Tips

1. **The single digitized register (008814402)** is in Spanish and unindexed — plan to work through it page by page, ideally with knowledge of colonial Spanish sacramental terminology.
2. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission directly** — they reportedly hold transcribed copies of the Spanish colonial materials not yet online.
3. **The Archivo General de Indias in Seville** holds the original Spanish Louisiana administrative records and is essential for deeper research into this period.
4. **FamilySearch's standard locality pages for Arkansas** are anchored to statehood (1836 onward) and offer little guidance for the Spanish colonial era — there is a genuine gap in online wiki coverage for this period.
5. **Mainstream genealogy websites (Ancestry, MyHeritage, etc.)** have essentially nothing specific to Arkansas Post before 1800. Do not expect to find this material through standard search interfaces.

---

**Bottom line:** Surviving records from Spanish-era Arkansas Post are sparse and scattered. The only material currently accessible online is a single browse-only, Spanish-language church register on FamilySearch. The most important next steps are to contact the **Arkansas History Commission** and the **Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** about their colonial holdings, and to have that digitized register reviewed page by page.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory era, c. 1788–1803, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787; Ohio did not become a state until 1803.
- **First counties:** Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790) were the first organized counties in the territory.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, under federal authority, prior to Ohio statehood.
- **Land systems:** Two distinct land-grant districts operated: the **Virginia Military District** (metes-and-bounds survey, reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans) and the **Connecticut Western Reserve** (gridded survey, northeastern Ohio).

---

## Boundary Changes
Boundary changes in this era were frequent. As new counties were carved out of the original Northwest Territory (Washington County in 1788, Hamilton County in 1790, and others before 1803), jurisdiction over any given tract shifted depending on when and where an event occurred. Researchers **must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event** — a land or court record from the 1790s may be filed under Washington County, Hamilton County, or still under the territorial government, depending on date and location.

---

## Available Record Types

### Land Records
- Two parallel systems (Virginia Military District and Connecticut Western Reserve), each with its own survey method and repository.
- **Virginia Military District warrants:** Virginia State Library.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve records:** Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Online:** *Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840* (FamilySearch collection 1542187, 234,567 people) covers this period. A volume of "Territorial Land Records" (Northwest Territory, 1788–1799) was found — 51 images, only 0% name-indexed, so it must be browsed image by image.

### Tax Records (Census Substitute)
- No federal census survives for Ohio before statehood in this window.
- A 73-image volume of "County Tax Records" for Washington County, Ohio, 1799–1803 exists — only 12% name-indexed, largely a browse exercise.
- *Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850* (FamilySearch collection 1987542, 345,890 people) begins just after 1800 but is worth checking for anyone still living at that time.

### Vital Records / Church Records
- No civil vital registration existed at the territorial level.
- *Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013* (FamilySearch collection 1803785, 3+ million people) reaches back into this window.
- *Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950* (FamilySearch collection 2246917, 678,234 people) begins right at the start of the target period. Church registers are the primary pre-registration alternative.

### Probate and Court Records
- **No digitized online collections** were found for probate/court records in this window. This is a digitization gap, **not** evidence the records don't exist — county court minute books from Washington and Hamilton Counties would be the place to look, held locally or at the **Ohio History Connection**.

---

## Known Record Losses
No tool result in this survey indicated that any specific Ohio record series from this period was destroyed. Absence of online hits should not be assumed to mean the records are lost.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collections | Gap it fills |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789–2013; Ohio, Church Records 1787–1950; Ohio, Land Records 1787–1840; Ohio, Tax Records 1800–1850 | Pre-statehood vital/land/tax coverage |
| National Archives (NARA) | Federal-level records | Federal records generally |
| Fold3 | Military records | Military service/pension gap |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial-location gap |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Local-notice gap |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Early territorial and county court/land records |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District warrants |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records |

---

## Research Tips
1. **Determine the county first.** Washington, Hamilton, or another county organized before 1803 — jurisdiction shifts by both date and location.
2. **Identify the land district.** Virginia Military District vs. Connecticut Western Reserve dictates which survey system and which repository to consult.
3. **Expect browse-only work.** Many digitized volumes for this period have little or no name indexing — plan to page through images rather than searching by name.
4. **Don't assume records are lost.** Probate and court records returned no online hits, but that reflects a digitization gap; contact the Ohio History Connection for access.

---

**In summary:** Researching Ohio ancestors around 1790 means working within the Northwest Territory's shifting county boundaries — records can be filed under Washington County, Hamilton County, or the territorial government itself depending on the exact year and location. Land records (split between two separate systems), tax lists, and some church and marriage records are partly available online, while court and estate records from this period likely survive only on paper at repositories like the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. A research plan can be built from this guide to sequence actual record searches for your specific ancestors.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory era, c. 1788–1803, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787; Ohio was not yet a state and would not become one until 1803 (per FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Washington County, organized in 1788, was the first county formed in the territory; Hamilton County followed in 1790 (same source).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, under federal authority, prior to Ohio statehood.
- **Population during period:** Population figures for this pre-1803 period were not returned by the population tool for "Ohio, United States" — the tool's data for this place begins only with statehood (1803), so no numeric population series is available here for 1780–1800.
- **Land systems:** Two distinct land-grant districts operated within what is now Ohio: the Virginia Military District (metes-and-bounds survey, reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans) and the Connecticut Western Reserve (gridded survey, northeastern Ohio) (FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

## Boundary changes
Boundary changes in this era were frequent and geographic, not a single clean before/after split: as new counties were organized out of the original Northwest Territory (Washington County in 1788, Hamilton County in 1790, and others before 1803), jurisdiction over any given tract shifted depending on where exactly it fell. The FamilySearch Wiki states plainly that researchers "must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory). Treat early Northwest Territory records and the later county-level Ohio records as one continuous research trail — an ancestor's land or court record from the 1790s may be filed under Washington or Hamilton County, or still under the territorial government, depending on date and location.

## Available record types

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Two parallel systems: the Virginia Military District and the Connecticut Western Reserve, each with its own survey method and its own record repository.
- **Where held:** Virginia Military District warrants are held at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records are held at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland (FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).
- **Digitized holdings found:** `collections_search` returned "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (collection 1542187, 234,567 people) covering this period. `volume_search` additionally found an image group of 51 images titled "Territorial Land Records" for the Northwest Territory, 1788–1799 — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, so it must be browsed image by image.

### Tax records (census substitute)
- No federal census survives for Ohio before statehood in this window. `volume_search` found a 73-image volume of "County Tax Records" for Washington County, Ohio, 1799–1803, only 12% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — largely a browse exercise. `collections_search` also lists "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (collection 1987542, 345,890 people), which begins just after this guide's window but is worth checking for anyone still alive into 1800.

### Vital records / church records
- No civil vital registration existed at the territorial level in this period; `collections_search` lists "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (collection 1803785, over 3 million people) which does reach back into this window, and "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (collection 2246917, 678,234 people), which begins right at the start of the target period. Church registers are the primary pre-registration alternative; no denomination-specific founding dates for this period were returned by the tools used here, so treat church coverage as a lead to pursue locally rather than a confirmed series.

### Probate and court records
- No digitized collection or catalog hit for probate/court records in this window was returned by `collections_search`, `volume_search`, or `catalog_search` (`catalog_search` for "Ohio, United States" returned zero hits). This is a cataloguing/digitization gap, not evidence the records don't exist — county court minute books from organized counties like Washington and Hamilton would be the place to look, held locally or at the Ohio History Connection.

## Records NOT online
- Probate, court-minute, and territorial administrative records for this period returned no online collections, volumes, or catalog hits in this survey. Land and tax records that do exist online are partly browse-only (see above).

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any specific Ohio record series from this period was destroyed; none should be assumed lost based on an absence of online hits alone.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789-2013 (1803785); Ohio, Church Records 1787-1950 (2246917); Ohio, Land Records 1787-1840 (1542187); Ohio, Tax Records 1800-1850 (1987542) | Pre-statehood vital/land/tax coverage | Free |
| National Archives (NARA) | General federal records reference | Federal-level records generally | https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | Military service/pension gap | https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial-location gap | https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Local-notice gap | https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only 2 digitized volumes matched Ohio/Northwest Territory, 1788–1803 in `volume_search`; no `summary` breakdown by record-type group was returned for this query, so counts of browse-only vs. full-text volumes beyond these two are not available from this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Early territorial and county court/land records | Named by the FamilySearch Wiki as the repository for these holdings — in-person or written request |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person / written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / written request |

## Research tips
- Determine the specific county (Washington, Hamilton, or others organized before 1803) that held jurisdiction over the ancestor's location at the time of the event, since the territory's boundaries shifted repeatedly in this period (FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).
- Identify which land district (Virginia Military District vs. Connecticut Western Reserve) the ancestor's land fell in before searching land records, since each uses a different survey system and a different repository (same source, #Land_Records).
- Where no digitized index exists (probate, court minutes, church registers), treat this as a digitization gap, not an absence of records, and plan to browse the relevant image volumes or contact the Ohio History Connection directly.
- The four general FamilySearch Wiki overview pages fetched for vital records, land and property, church records, and census returned only generic, non-place-specific template content with no Ohio-specific dates or figures — do not treat anything from those pages as an Ohio-specific finding.

---
This survey looked at the Ohio region in the years just before it became a state, roughly 1788 to 1803, when it was part of the Northwest Territory and its county boundaries were still being drawn and redrawn; what's available from that time is mostly land records (split between two separate record-keeping systems depending on where exactly the land was), some tax lists, and church and marriage records, while court and estate records from this period were not found in any online index and likely exist only on paper at places like the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. The most important thing to know is that records can be filed under whichever county existed at the exact time and place of the event, so tracing an ancestor often means checking Washington County, Hamilton County, and the territorial government in turn, and being ready to browse unindexed image collections page by page rather than searching by name.

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to sequence the actual record searches for your specific ancestors.
