output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview

French colonial Louisiana was established after La Salle's 1682 Mississippi basin claim; New Orleans was founded in 1718. The territory passed through several sovereigns within your research window:
- **France** (1682–1762)
- **Spain** (1762–1800, Treaty of Fontainebleau)
- **France briefly** (1800–1803)
- **United States** (Louisiana Purchase, 1803)

A single family's records may appear under French, Spanish, or early American administration depending on the year — treat these as one continuous trail rather than separate systems.

The **Catholic Church** was the only legally recognized denomination in French Louisiana, making Catholic parish registers the primary genealogical source for the entire period.

---

## Key Record Types

### Church Records (Most Important for This Era)
- **What exists:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials in Catholic parish registers
- **Significance:** The *Code Noir* (Black Code) mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons — parish registers are therefore also a primary source for tracing enslaved ancestors
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** has registers from **1720**
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection id 1612905)
- **Digitized images:** Image group 004330991 covers sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, in French and Spanish**
- **Note:** No statewide civil vital registration existed before 1819; church records are the only vital-event source for this era

### Colonial Government / Court Records (Superior Council)
- The **Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council)** records include land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories
- Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans); partially digitized
- Digitized image group 004330992 covers French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council), 1699–1769 — **browse-only, 0% indexed, in French and Spanish**
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection id 2078341) covers the tail of this period

### Notarial Records
- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** (oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the **1730s** onward
- These can supply family relationships not found in parish registers alone
- Access: in-person at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center

### Land Records
- French/Spanish land grants ("concessions") follow French/Spanish legal tradition — not U.S. rectangular survey
- Documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and at the **Louisiana State Land Office**
- Also in the Superior Council records noted above

### Census / Administrative Records
- No U.S. federal census during this period (federal census begins 1790, and Louisiana wasn't yet U.S. territory)
- French administrative census rolls and colonial correspondence are held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — this may require travel or a research agent, as no online access was confirmed

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Relevant Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1718–1925 (id 1612905); Probate Records 1756–1984 (id 2078341); browse-only image groups for sacramental registers (004330991) and Superior Council notarial acts (004330992) | Free |
| **FamilySearch Wiki** | "Louisiana Genealogy" — French Colonial Records section | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, estate inventories |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral** | Parish sacramental registers from 1720 |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France** | Colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Colonial land grant documentation |

---

## Important Gaps and Cautions

- **No name-indexes** for either major digitized colonial image group — both must be browsed image by image
- Both digitized collections are in **French and/or Spanish** — plan for reading in those languages
- Some Superior Council records and all ANOM (France) colonial materials are **not yet online**
- No specific record losses or fires were identified by this survey; lack of indexing reflects digitization gaps, not destroyed records
- Sovereignty changes mean you must search under French naming conventions, Spanish naming conventions, and early American forms for the same family

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Catholic parish registers** — specifically the St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (FamilySearch image group 004330992), browsing by estimated date range
2. **Don't stop at church records** — the New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts and marriage settlements with family relationships not always found in registers
3. **Account for the name change:** French names were often Hispanicized under Spanish rule (1762–1800) and may appear differently in those decades
4. **For enslaved ancestors:** The Code Noir baptism requirement makes parish registers your best entry point; also look in estate inventories in the Superior Council records
5. **For French colonial administrative and census material** not in New Orleans, plan for ANOM in France — no online access to those records was confirmed

The natural next step would be to build a research plan starting with the Catholic parish registers and Superior Council records for a specific person or family.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French colonial Louisiana was established as part of New France following La Salle's 1682 claim to the Mississippi basin; New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville (Wikipedia: French Louisiana).
- **Administrative seat:** New Orleans (after 1722); earlier colonial administration was based at Mobile and Biloxi.
- **Parent jurisdiction / sovereignty changes:** France controlled the territory 1682–1762; Spain administered it 1762–1800 under the Treaty of Fontainebleau (France retained the eastern portion, ceded to Britain); France briefly regained it in 1800 before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. This means a single family's records in this window may be filed under French, Spanish, or early American administration depending on the exact year.
- **Economy/society:** Plantation agriculture, fur trade, and enslaved labor under the Code Noir (Black Code), which mandated Catholic baptism of enslaved people — a key genealogical hook for tracing enslaved ancestors (Wikipedia: French Louisiana).
- **Religious context:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized denomination in French Louisiana, making Catholic parish registers the primary genealogical source for the entire period (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" — French Colonial Records section, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).

## Boundary changes
French Louisiana was reorganized administratively multiple times (France to 1762, Spain 1762–1800, briefly France again in 1800, then the United States from 1803). Records for the same family may therefore appear under French colonial administration (Superior Council), Spanish colonial administration, or early American territorial administration depending on the exact date — treat this as one continuous record trail rather than separate systems. I could not confirm an exact parish-level civil boundary history from the FamilySearch Wiki in this survey (see Gaps below); the `Louisiana_Vital_Records`, `Louisiana_Church_Records`, and `Louisiana_Land_and_Property` pages I attempted all returned only generic, non-jurisdiction-specific template content rather than Louisiana-specific detail, so I am not citing dates from them.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No FamilySearch Wiki page returned Louisiana-specific civil registration start dates in this survey — the pages fetched returned only generic boilerplate content, not Louisiana detail. I cannot state a reliable statewide civil registration start date from this survey.
- **What exists instead:** A FamilySearch collection, "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection id 1543892, 2,345,678 persons), begins in 1819 — after the French colonial period, confirming no statewide civil vital registration existed during 1699–1803.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Catholic parish registers (see Church records below) are the only vital-event source for this era.

### Church records
- **Denomination present:** Catholic Church only (legally the sole recognized church in French Louisiana) (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials; the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons, so parish registers also document enslaved ancestors.
- **Specific holdings:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans, has registers from 1720 (same source as above). FamilySearch's digitized collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection id 1612905, 987,654 persons) covers this period and is listed in `collections_search`.
- **Digitized images:** A `volume_search` hit, image group 004330991, covers "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans" for Orleans, Louisiana, 1720–1803 (264 images). It is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse-only images — and in **French and Spanish**, so the researcher must read the original language and browse image by image.
- **Gaps:** No separate online index was found for this collection beyond browse access; treat it as browse-only per the volume_search result above.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French and Spanish land grants ("concessions") followed French/Spanish legal tradition rather than U.S. rectangular survey or metes-and-bounds common law. Colonial land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property" — Colonial Land Grants section, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Notarial archives:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward, accessible via the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (same source).
- **Digitized images:** `volume_search` image group 004330992 covers "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)" for Louisiana, 1699–1769 (149 images), **0% indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish** — browse-only.

### Probate and court records
- **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur):** Records include land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories, held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, and partially digitized (same FamilySearch Wiki source as Church records above).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection id 2078341, 456,789 persons) overlaps the tail of this period (1756 onward).
- **Testate/intestate:** Not specified by any tool result for this period; search both wills and administrations/estate inventories in the Superior Council records.

### Census records
- The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for French colonial Louisiana (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records). No U.S. federal or state census existed for this period; the earliest colonial census data is French administrative, not a standard enumeration.
- `place_population` returned no data for Louisiana in 1700–1803 in this survey — a data gap, not evidence of no population.

### Military records
- No Louisiana-specific colonial military records were surfaced by any tool in this survey. General U.S. military record guidance (NARA) applies only from the American period onward (post-1803) and is not directly applicable to French/Spanish colonial service, which would instead be documented in French/Spanish archives (see ANOM above).

### Immigration/emigration records
- No port-specific colonial immigration records were returned by any tool in this survey; passenger/settler records for this era would likely be in French or Spanish colonial administrative archives (ANOM) rather than U.S. immigration series, which postdate this period.

### Newspaper and cemetery records
- No Louisiana colonial-period newspapers or cemetery collections were returned by any tool in this survey for 1699–1803; newspapers and organized cemetery recordkeeping are generally later developments in this region.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (id 1612905, 987,654 persons); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (id 2078341, 456,789 persons); "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (id 1543892, 2,345,678 persons); "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957" (id 1798054, 1,135,780 persons); digitized image groups 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803, browse-only) and 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769, browse-only) | No statewide civil vital registration before 1819 — church records fill this | Free |
| FamilySearch Wiki | Category: Vital Records | General vital-records orientation | Free |
| Find A Grave | findagrave.com | Cemetery records (no colonial-specific data confirmed) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | newspapers.com | Newspaper records (no colonial-period Louisiana titles confirmed) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | fold3.com | Military records (post-colonial period primarily) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Census (federal census begins 1790, not colonial) | Subscription |
| NARA | archives.gov | Federal-era records (post-1803) | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized image volumes total for Louisiana in 1699–1803 (both browse-only, French/Spanish language) — this is the complete result set for that query, not a partial page. `catalog_search` for "Louisiana, United States" returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap in this tool's index, not evidence that no colonial records exist (the FamilySearch Wiki prose and volume_search results above describe real holdings for this period).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories | In-person; partially digitized |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts, contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s | In-person; public access research center |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans archives / St. Louis Cathedral | Parish sacramental registers from 1720 | In-person / via FamilySearch microfilm |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls | In-person in France; some materials may be microfilmed elsewhere (not confirmed by any tool result here) |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grant documentation | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
The Superior Council records (land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories) are described as only "partially digitized" — the remainder exists only at the Louisiana Historical Center. The ANOM colonial administrative correspondence and census rolls in France were not shown by any tool result to be digitized or online. Full-text search and name-indexing are not available for either digitized colonial image group found (sacramental registers or notarial acts) — both are browse-only.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported a specific record loss, fire, or destruction for Louisiana's French colonial records. I am not asserting any loss — absence of online indexing for these collections is a digitization gap, not a statement that records were destroyed.

## Research tips
- Because sovereignty changed hands during this period (French to 1762, Spanish 1762–1800, French again briefly, then American from 1803), search for the same family across all three administrative naming conventions and recordkeeping systems rather than assuming one applies throughout (Wikipedia: French Louisiana).
- The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved people, so parish sacramental registers are also a primary source for tracing enslaved ancestors in this period (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- Both key digitized colonial image groups (sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts) are in French and/or Spanish and must be browsed image by image with no name index — plan for language-reading time and browse systematically by date rather than searching by name.
- Attempts to fetch the FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana-specific Vital Records, Church Records, and Land and Property pages in this survey returned only generic template content, not Louisiana-specific detail; treat start dates and specifics from those pages as unconfirmed, and rely instead on the wiki_search excerpts cited above.
- For French/Spanish administrative and census material not held in New Orleans, the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in France is the named repository — factor in that this likely requires either travel or a research agent, as no digitization or online access was confirmed by any tool here.
- Use the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for contracts, marriage settlements, and property records from the 1730s onward, which can supply family relationships not found in parish registers alone.

---
This survey covers the whole state of Louisiana during the years when it was a French and then Spanish colony, roughly 1699 to 1803. The main surviving records from that era are Catholic church registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials (the only recognized church at the time), plus colonial government records called the "Superior Council" records covering land grants, court cases, and estate matters, along with notarial contracts kept in New Orleans going back to the 1730s; some of these have been scanned by FamilySearch but can only be browsed page by page, not searched by name, and are written in French or Spanish. A few important gaps to know about: no routine state birth, marriage, or death registration existed until 1819, so church records are essential for anything earlier; Louisiana's rulers changed from French to Spanish and briefly back to French before becoming American territory, so a family's records may be filed differently depending on the exact year; and some original colonial government records survive only in physical archives in New Orleans or in France, not online.

The natural next step is to have a research plan built around these church, notarial, and colonial-government record sets, ideally starting with the Catholic parish registers of New Orleans.

- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births and deaths began in 1906 (level: state); before that, Philadelphia recorded locally from 1860 and Allegheny County from 1870 (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). - **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family Bibles, and county marriage license/bond records (county level, colonial period onward).

### Church records
- **Collection:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people) - this is a county-specific collection and covers the entire 1840-1908 target window.

- external_links_search returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general cemetery-records resource for this place.

- external_links_search returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a general resource; no Schuylkill-specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not independently covered by tool results in this survey; coal-region immigrant families (many from Ireland, Wales, Germany, and later Eastern Europe) generated naturalization and alien-registration paperwork inland, but no Schuylkill-specific source was returned.

### Occupational/industry records (mining)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards** (image group 002240015, 1870-1900, 410 images): 95% name-indexed AND full-text searchable - for Schuylkill County specifically. This is the strongest single record set this survey found for a mining ancestor.

- Search the Mine Worker Employment Cards (1870-1900) first for a mining ancestor - it is the only fully name-indexed, full-text-searchable collection this survey found specific to Schuylkill County.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Anthracite Coal Region) (1840-1908)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811, from parts of Berks and Northampton Counties (per place_search dateRange +1811/)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Economy:** Dominant anthracite coal mining industry, reflected in dedicated Mine Worker Employment Cards, Mine Accident Reports, and Colliery Payroll Ledgers collections for this region
- **Note:** place_population and place_search_all returned no data for this place in this survey - population figures and a full jurisdictional-change list are not available from these tools here

## Boundary changes
place_search_all returned no historical-jurisdiction results for Schuylkill County in this survey; no boundary change could be confirmed or ruled out from tool output. Treat Schuylkill as the operative county for the whole 1840-1908 period absent further evidence.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births and deaths began in 1906 (level: state); before that, Philadelphia recorded locally from 1860 and Allegheny County from 1870 (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). No separate start date is stated for Schuylkill County itself.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (id 2255317, 4,218,763 people) covers the tail of the target period (1906-1908) at the state level.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates post-1906 are state-level; pre-1906, no civil death/birth series is confirmed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family Bibles, and county marriage license/bond records (county level, colonial period onward).

### Church records
- **Collection:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people) - county-specific and covers the entire 1840-1908 target window.
- **Denominations present:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey; the wiki place-pages returned only generic content, so no specific congregation list is confirmed.
- **Language:** Not stated by tool output; many coal-region parishes (Irish, Welsh, German, Slavic, Lithuanian) kept records in languages other than English, but this survey found no source confirming which applied to Schuylkill specifically.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available 1840-1900 (decennial); no Schuylkill-specific gaps were found by any tool call in this survey.
- **Access:** Not independently itemized by collections_search in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- **Collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196, dateRange 1683-1994) is state-level and overlaps the full target period, but its personCount returned as 0 - likely unindexed/browse-only.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills, per general FamilySearch Wiki guidance; no Schuylkill-specific repository location was confirmed by a tool result.

### Land records
- Not independently covered by this survey's tool results; generic wiki content named county courthouses and the state Land Office as general PA repositories, with no Schuylkill-specific detail.

### Military records
- No Schuylkill-specific collection, volume, or catalog hit was returned by any tool in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- external_links_search returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general cemetery-records resource for this place.

### Newspaper records
- external_links_search returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a general resource; no Schuylkill-specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not independently covered by tool results in this survey; coal-region immigrant families (many from Ireland, Wales, Germany, and later Eastern Europe) generated naturalization and alien-registration paperwork inland, but no Schuylkill-specific source was returned.

### Occupational/industry records (mining)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards** (image group 002240015, 1870-1900, 410 images): 95% name-indexed AND full-text searchable for Schuylkill County specifically. This is the strongest single record set this survey found for a mining ancestor.
- **Mine Accident Reports** (image group 002240016, 1870-1895, 287 images), coverage for Luzerne County: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable - browse-only.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers** (image group 002240017, 1878-1900, 199 images), coverage for Lackawanna County: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable - browse-only.
- volume_search reported 23 total matching volumes for this region/period; only 3 were detailed above - the rest were not examined in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Schuylkill County Church Records (982,415 people, 1708-1985); PA County Marriages 1885-1950; PA Probate Records 1683-1994; PA Death Certificates 1906-1968; PA Civil Marriages 1677-1950; PA Compiled Marriages 1700-1900; Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill, 1870-1900) | Pre-1906 vital-record gap (church/marriage collections); post-1906 deaths; mining-employment history | Free |

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** was founded in 1628; **Plymouth Colony** (1620) was separate until they merged in 1691 under a new royal charter.
- The **Great Migration (1630–1640)** brought roughly 20,000 Puritan settlers under Governor John Winthrop.
- Congregational (Puritan) churches dominated religious life and kept their own records.
- **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** generated militia rolls relevant to this period.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Town-Level)
- Massachusetts required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — this was a town-level, not statewide, mandate.
- The published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series covers 200+ towns.
- **Online:** FamilySearch's *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (collection id 2061550, ~3.46 million persons, indexed).

### Church Records
- Congregational churches kept membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings from the colony's founding.
- **Online:** FamilySearch's *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (id 1921657, ~987,654 persons, indexed).
- One specific digitized volume (image group 007612045, Suffolk County, 1630–1700, Congregational admissions and baptisms) is **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — it must be searched by keyword or browsed page by page.

### Town Meeting / Proprietors' Records
- Image group 007612044 (188 images, Massachusetts, 1620–1698) covers land grants, town governance, and inhabitant lists.
- This volume is **browse-only** — 0% indexed and not full-text searchable. Must be paged through image by image.

### Probate Records
- Probate courts began in the 1630s.
- **Online:** FamilySearch's *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (id 1678901, ~567,890 persons, indexed).
- Includes wills, inventories, and administrations.

### Land Records
- County-level deed books survive from the **1630s** in "remarkably complete runs."
- Town-level grants also appear in proprietors' records (see above).
- **Held at:** County registries of deeds; original colony records at the Massachusetts Archives.

### Military Records
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) militia rolls are partially published.
- **Held at:** Massachusetts Archives; partially online.

### Court Records
- County courts and the General Court handled criminal, civil, and administrative matters from the colony's founding.
- **Held at:** Massachusetts Archives.

### Immigration Records — Important Gap
- No passenger lists survive for the 1620s–1630s Great Migration in FamilySearch's indexed holdings for this period. The standard substitute is **published compiled genealogies** — consult NEHGS for Great Migration research.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records, 1620–1890; Church Records, 1630–1920; Probate Records, 1635–1991 | Free |
| FamilySearch (unindexed) | Town meeting/proprietors' records, image group 007612044 (browse-only) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal-level records | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** | Original colony records from the 1620s, probate, court, military rolls |
| **County registries of deeds** | Land/deed books from the 1630s |
| **County probate courts** | Wills, inventories, administrations from the 1630s |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Largest genealogical library in the region; Great Migration research |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search by town first.** Puritan vital registration began at the town level in 1639 — always identify your ancestor's specific town before searching.

2. **Know which colony applies.** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony were *separate jurisdictions* until 1691 — confirm which colony your ancestor's town belonged to.

3. **Church records fill gaps in civil records.** Membership and disciplinary records can supply family relationships not found in town vital records. The Suffolk County Congregational admissions/baptisms volume (image group 007612045) is worth checking for that area.

4. **For the Great Migration itself,** no indexed passenger lists exist for the 1620s–1630s. Turn to NEHGS and published Great Migration compilations instead.

5. **Browse the town meeting volume.** Image group 007612044 contains inhabitant lists and land grants but requires page-by-page browsing — it cannot be name-searched.

6. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly** for Massachusetts-specific research articles: [Massachusetts Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)

7. **NEHGS** is the premier resource for New England genealogy in this period and holds compiled genealogies, published town records, and Great Migration research not fully available digitally.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run era, 1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma became a state in 1907; from 1889–1907, the settled area was **Oklahoma Territory** (opened April 22, 1889) and **Indian Territory** to the east — two separate jurisdictions until their merger at statehood.
- **Key historical events:** The Land Run of 1889 and subsequent openings (1891, 1892, 1893 Cherokee Outlet, 1901 lottery) rapidly settled the territory. Indian Territory remained under tribal/federal jurisdiction until the 1907 merger.

---

## Boundary Changes
Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were distinct jurisdictions until 1907. Early records may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" rather than the modern state name, and **tribal-roll records** for Indian Territory families are a separate record stream — search both chains for families near the territorial border.

---

## Available Record Types

### Land Records (Homestead / Land Run Records) ⭐ *Start here*
- **What exists:** Homestead applications, final proofs, and land patents generated by the Run. Each file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement (with witnesses), and the final patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and can contain family details.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office); patents also at **glorecords.blm.gov** (BLM General Land Office site).
- **Indexed collection:** FamilySearch collection **1541872**, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — 234,567 people indexed.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group **005221388** — "Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs," Oklahoma, 1889–1907, 402 images, 74% name-indexed (browse the rest).

### Census / Rolls
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census:** One of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations in the nation (the national 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed). Held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** — an unusually valuable substitute.
- **Indian Territory Rolls:** FamilySearch collection **1987432**, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" — 567,890 people. Related image group **005221389** — "Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910" — 176 images, **browse-only** (0% indexed).

### Marriage Records
- **Indexed collection:** FamilySearch collection **2134789**, "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" — 913,578 people, held at the county level.

### Church Records
- Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in new towns.
- **Indexed collection:** FamilySearch collection **1654321**, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" — 123,456 people (the 1820 start reflects earlier Indian Territory mission-era records).

### Court and Probate Records
- Territorial district courts (1890–1907) handled civil, criminal, probate, and naturalization matters.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives.

### Migration Origins
- Many Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states**. Plan to search those states' land, census, and county records *before 1889* to trace the family's origins before the Run.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1541872, 1987432, 2134789, 1654321; digitized image groups 005221388 and 005221389 | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Original land patent images | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives, Washington, D.C. (RG 49) | Original homestead case files, land patents |
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory district court records |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census, territorial records |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial court records |

---

## Records NOT Online
Original homestead case files (NARA Washington) and territorial district court records (NARA Fort Worth / Oklahoma State Archives) were not shown as digitized — plan written requests or an in-person visit.

---

## Key Research Tips
1. **Search both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory records separately** before 1907 — they were distinct jurisdictions with different record systems.
2. **Check rejected homestead applications** too — they can contain detailed family information.
3. **Use the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** at the Oklahoma Historical Society to bridge the gap left by the destroyed national 1890 census.
4. **Trace settlers' origin states** (Kansas, Texas, Missouri) before assuming the family began in Oklahoma — many settlers migrated from those states just before or during the Run.
5. The FamilySearch Catalog returned 0 hits for Oklahoma in this tool session — this is a cataloguing gap in the tool, not proof no microfilm exists; check the Catalog directly at familysearch.org.

---

If you'd like, I can build a research plan targeting a specific family using these sources, or help you survey the origin states (Kansas, Texas, Missouri) for pre-1889 records.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Mississippi Territory (1798–1819, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The area that became Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (organized 1798), carved from land ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. It became the separate **Alabama Territory** in 1817 and achieved statehood in 1819.

**Key early counties:** County formation began with Adams and Pickering counties in 1799; **Washington County (1800)** covered most of present-day Alabama, with Baldwin (1809), Madison (1808), and Mobile (1812) later carved from it.

**Parent jurisdiction:** United States territorial government, administered from Natchez, then St. Stephens.

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical for Researchers

This region presents a layered jurisdictional problem:
- Pre-1817 records may be filed under **"Mississippi Territory"** rather than "Alabama"
- **Washington County** was the original umbrella county for most of the Alabama portion of the territory, later subdivided into Baldwin, Madison, and Mobile counties
- Tracing which successor county holds a specific record depends on exactly where within old Washington County the event occurred

---

## Available Record Types

### Territorial Census Records
- Territorial census enumerations were taken in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816**, held at the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** (Jackson) and the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery)
- **Online substitute:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (FamilySearch collection id 2016756, 287,634 people) and "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890" (id 1927171, 198,340 people)

### Land Records — Strongest Source for This Period
- Federal land sales began in **1803** through the **St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices**; original files are at the National Archives (Record Group 49) and indexed on the **BLM General Land Office website**
- **Online:** "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (FamilySearch collection id 1919694, 312,450 people) — covers the full 1798–1819 window; this is the strongest confirmed online source for this period

### Church Records
- **Online:** "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (FamilySearch id 1986396, 156,789 people) — overlaps the tail of this period (1803–1819)
- **Online:** "Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950" (FamilySearch id 2034891, 87,654 people)

### Probate and Court Records
- **Online:** "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (FamilySearch id 1537764, 438,210 people) — covers 1809–1819
- **Online:** "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (FamilySearch id 1855293, 245,670 people) — covers nearly the entire target period and includes Washington County-era business for the Alabama portion of the territory

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **None existed** in any systematic form for this early frontier period. Church records and county court/probate records are the substitute sources.

### Military Records
- No specific collection for the Creek War (1813–1814) or other conflicts in this period was confirmed by the tools used in this survey.

---

## Digitized, Browsable Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

You specifically asked about digitized, browsable (even unindexed) volumes. Unfortunately, **`volume_search` and `catalog_search` both returned zero results** for this place and period:

- `volume_search` for "Alabama, United States" (1798–1819) → **0 results**
- `volume_search` for "Mississippi Territory, United States" over the same years → **0 results**
- `catalog_search` for both place names → **0 hits**

> **This is a cataloguing/coverage gap in the online tools, not evidence that no such volumes exist anywhere.** It simply means no digitized browsable image volumes for this exact place and period were surfaced by the FamilySearch catalog tools used here.

**Recommended next steps for browsable volumes:**
1. Check the **FamilySearch Catalog directly** at [familysearch.org/catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search) under "Mississippi Territory" and each early Alabama county
2. Contact the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery) directly — they hold the territorial census enumerations and likely other physical record volumes not yet scanned
3. Contact the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** (Jackson) — same reasoning

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Period Covered |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (online) | Land, church, probate, court, census substitutes (7 collections) | 1798–1819 |
| Alabama Dept. of Archives & History | Territorial census enumerations, county records | 1800–1819 |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History | Territorial census enumerations, territorial records | 1798–1817 |
| National Archives (RG 49) | Federal land entry files | 1803–1819 |
| BLM GLO website | Land patents and entry files | 1803+ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (general) | — |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search both "Alabama" and "Mississippi Territory"** — a record for an Alabama location may be filed under the Mississippi Territory place name, since statehood didn't come until 1819.
2. **Trace county succession carefully** — Washington County (1800) was the original umbrella, later split into Baldwin, Madison, and Mobile counties. Search all of them if your ancestor's location is uncertain.
3. **Start with land records** — The BLM GLO site and FamilySearch's Mississippi Territorial/State Land Records collection (id 1919694) are the most richly populated online sources for this period.
4. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama** did not return jurisdiction-specific detail for this early period during this survey — check them directly on the live site, and also look up "Mississippi Territory Genealogy" on the wiki for more territorial-era guidance.
5. **No confirmed online browse-only volumes exist** via the catalog tools — physical repository contact is the path forward for unindexed image browsing.

The useful records from that era are mostly land records, probate and county court papers, church registers, and a few territorial population counts (taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816), and these are described as being held at the Alabama and Mississippi state archives and at county courthouses, plus a set of indexed online collections on FamilySearch covering church, probate, court, census-substitute, and land records that each touch part of this period; however, the tools I used to specifically check for digitized "browse it yourself, no name search" record volumes and for microfilm/catalog holdings came back completely empty for this place and time, so right now there is no confirmed online scan you can simply flip through for this early period, and the FamilySearch Wiki's own detailed pages for Alabama did not return specific information during this check. The most important thing to know is that because this region was shared between two territories before Alabama became its own state, and the local counties were repeatedly split and renamed, records for one ancestor could be filed under either Alabama or Mississippi territorial names and under several different county names, so the next step would be to have a research plan built that searches both place names and all the successor counties, and to contact the state archives directly about any physical, unscanned volumes.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1860s-1890s), Anthracite Coal Region

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811, standardPlace "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States".
- **Population:** 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (US Census).
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; attracted Irish immigrant labor from the 1830s onward, especially post-Famine.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish miners dominated the workforce in the 1840s-50s; later Eastern European immigration.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European communities (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records).
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires secret society active among Irish miners 1860s-1870s, generating court records, trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and families (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy).

## Scope note
The anthracite coal region comprises five counties: Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. This guide surveys Schuylkill County only, per the subject's death location. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon still need their own locality-guide surveys.

## Boundary changes
No boundary change was identified for Schuylkill County itself during 1860s-1890s; it was formed in 1811 and the standardPlace carries no later jurisdiction change.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Vital Records page could not be retrieved specifically - the fetch returned only a generic "Genealogy_Records" fallback page with no Pennsylvania-specific start date. Treat statewide registration date as unconfirmed by this survey.
- **What exists:** A browse-only Marriage Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753), 94 images, 1870-1910, English, 0% indexed.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized microfilm (browse-only).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes serving Irish immigrants, established 1840-1870 (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials implied by parish registers; a Church Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936751), 187 images, 1842-1895, in English and German, 0% indexed, browse-only.
- **Where held:** Before 1868 all five anthracite counties (including Schuylkill) fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia; Schuylkill and Carbon remained with Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961 (so Schuylkill parish registers for the full 1860s-1890s target period are Philadelphia diocesan records) (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records).
- **Collection:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (collection id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), 1708-1985, 982,415 persons (collections_search).
- **Gaps:** No separate index for non-Catholic denominations was returned by this survey.
- **Language:** English and German for the digitized Church Records volume; Catholic registers may be in Latin (not confirmed by a tool result).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 population figures confirmed (place_population); 1890 federal census is famously destroyed nationwide (background knowledge, not confirmed by a tool result here - flagged as background only).
- **Access:** An 1850 Schuylkill County federal census index is available via Ancestry (external_links_search, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/).
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state assessors took triennial tax assessments from 1853 (see Tax records).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories (implied).
- **Where held:** A Probate Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936749), 412 images, 1851-1930, 0% indexed, browse-only, FamilySearch. Also "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection id 1999196, 0 indexed persons returned) via collections_search.
- **Molly Maguires court records:** Trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton detective reports from the 1860s-1870s name hundreds of Irish-born miners and families (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Molly Maguires section).

### Land records
- **Types:** Deeds. A Deed Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936752), 543 images, 1815-1900, 22% name-indexed (not fully indexed), browse remainder, FamilySearch.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any tool result retrieved in this survey; a specific Land and Property wiki page was not fetched in this pass.

### Military records
- Not surveyed with a specific tool result in this pass; the generic FamilySearch Wiki template notes service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations are held at the National Archives.

### Cemetery records
- Not surveyed with a specific tool result in this pass.

### Newspaper records
- Molly Maguires trial coverage generated extensive newspaper coverage per FamilySearch Wiki (Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy); no specific paper titles or date ranges were returned by a tool in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Types:** Naturalization Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936750), 298 images, 1849-1915, 0% indexed, browse-only, FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Full manifests, when located, should be checked for all family members including children.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state assessors took triennial assessments from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records). A separate "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" is available via Ancestry (external_links_search, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) but predates the 1860s-1890s target period - background only.
- **Substitute value:** Useful between census years and especially for the missing 1890 federal census.

### Other record types
- **Colliery employment records:** The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds payroll ledgers for several collieries (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Coal Mining Records section).
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books surviving a 1903 records consolidation; entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). Note: this index's title names the Lackawanna Valley (lower anthracite field); its applicability to Schuylkill County workers specifically is not confirmed by the page and should be checked directly.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records vol. 007936751 (1842-1895, browse-only); Probate vol. 007936749; Naturalization vol. 007936750; Deed vol. 007936752 (22% indexed); Marriage vol. 007936753; "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (982,415 persons); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" | Browse-only church, probate, naturalization and marriage images not otherwise indexed | Free |
| Ancestry | "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (collection 1276) | 1850 census index for the county | Subscription |
| Ancestry | "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (collection 7667) | Pre-period tax substitute, background only | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes matched Schuylkill County for 1860-1900 and all 5 are detailed above (volume_search reported complete: true, no further page).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Colliery payroll ledgers for several collieries | Not stated by a tool result; contact the Society directly |
| Diocese of Philadelphia archives | Pre-1868 (and Schuylkill/Carbon post-1868 until 1961) Catholic parish baptismal/marriage/burial registers | Not stated by a tool result; contact the archdiocesan archive directly |
| Schuylkill County courthouse | Probate, deed, naturalization originals underlying the browse-only FamilySearch volumes | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Colliery payroll ledgers (Historical Society of Schuylkill County) - not digitized per any tool result in this survey.
- Probate, naturalization, deed (78% unindexed), marriage, and church-record volumes above are online as browse-only images, not name-searchable.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified a specific destroyed record set for Schuylkill County. (The 1890 federal census's nationwide loss is general background knowledge, not confirmed by a tool call in this survey, and is flagged as such above.)

## Research tips
- Distinguish company payroll indexes (name individual colliery workers) from mine-inspection/accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person) - the payroll-derived indexes are the more useful finding aid for immigrant miners inconsistently indexed in census records (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- For pre-1868 (and Schuylkill/Carbon post-1868) Catholic baptismal registers, search the Diocese of Philadelphia archives, not a Scranton or Harrisburg diocesan collection (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records).
- The Molly Maguires court and newspaper record trail (trial transcripts, depositions, Pinkerton reports) names many Irish-born miners and families and is worth searching directly by surname (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires).
- Check the Historical Society of Schuylkill County directly for colliery payroll ledgers, since they are not described as digitized by any tool result here.
- This survey's four generic FamilySearch Wiki place-research pages (home/getting_started/online_records/research_tips) returned only boilerplate content, not place-specific facts - re-check the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Schuylkill-specific research-tips content.
- Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon counties (the rest of the anthracite region) still need their own locality-guide surveys.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, Late 1700s)

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

Vermont was admitted as the **14th state in 1791**, per the FamilySearch Wiki's [Vermont Genealogy page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). Before that, the territory's land was granted under competing authorities: **New Hampshire** issued town grants; **New York** claimed jurisdiction over the same land and refused to recognize those grants — the dispute that produced the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.

FamilySearch's own place index dates "Vermont, United States" only from 1791 and returned no distinct pre-1791 jurisdictional entry in this search. The specific predecessor county/jurisdiction under New York's administration needs to be identified from sources outside this session's results.

---

## Boundary Changes

No tool result in this run named which specific colonial jurisdiction (e.g., Albany County, New York, or the NY-organized Cumberland/Gloucester Counties) held civil records for the Vermont territory before 1791. That is a genuine gap to investigate further — do not assume a specific predecessor county without further lookup.

---

## Available Record Types

### 🏆 Key Pre-Statehood Source: Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule
- Prepared under New York colonial authority; enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of the disputed New Hampshire grants
- Each entry includes: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status
- This is the **earliest systematic resident list** for the area — predating all civil registration
- Where held: not stated in this run's results; the FamilySearch Catalog search returned zero matches, which is a gap in this run, not evidence the record is inaccessible

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **Statewide civil registration** began in **1857**
- Some **town clerk records** survive back to the 1770s, but survival is **uneven**
- Custodian: **town clerk offices directly** — no statewide/archival aggregation exists for this era
- For the pre-statehood period, town clerk records and the 1771 Schedule are the named substitutes; church registers were not addressed by this run's Vermont-specific results

### Land Records
- Pre-statehood land was distributed under competing New Hampshire and New York grant authority
- Town histories (mostly published 1860–1900) often **reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** and may be the only accessible copy of that material

### Census Records
- The **1790 federal census** is the one federal enumeration touching this pre-statehood window (Vermont was not yet a state when taken)
- No separate Vermont colonial/state census for the 1770s–1791 period was found in this run

### Church, Probate, Court, Military, Cemetery, Newspaper, Immigration, Tax Records
No Vermont-specific findings for these record types in the 1760s–1791 period were returned by this run's tools. These categories should be followed up independently.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
FamilySearch's **collections search**, **catalog**, and **digitized-volume search** all returned zero results for "Vermont, United States" in the 1760–1791 range. This is a coverage/indexing gap in this search run — not evidence that no such records are digitized. General starting points returned:
- U.S. Federal Census Collection — [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)
- [FamilySearch — Vital Records category](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records)
- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/)
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)
- [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) *(military records)*
- [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/)

None of these returned a Vermont-specific collection or date range in this run.

### Physical Repositories
No specific physical repository (state archives, county courthouse, historical society) was named by this run's tools. The FamilySearch Wiki names only **town clerk offices** for pre-1857 records.

---

## Records Not Online / Known Losses

- Pre-1857 town clerk vital records are described as surviving **unevenly** and not aggregated anywhere online — direct contact with individual towns is required
- No online collection for the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule was returned by this run
- No documented destruction events were identified, only uneven survival

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — it is the earliest resident list and predates all civil registration for the territory.
2. **Contact town clerk offices directly** — they are the stated custodians of any surviving 1770s vital records; there is no single statewide index.
3. **Search town histories (1860–1900)** — these often reprint colonial proprietors' records that survive nowhere else.
4. **Don't confuse pre- and post-statehood series** — the FamilySearch Wiki opens with this caution; records before 1791 follow colonial patterns, not state ones.
5. **Identify the predecessor New York county** — civil and legal records before statehood were kept by whatever New York county administered the area; that county is the right place to look for probate, court, and deed records.
6. **Re-run catalog and collection searches** — this session's FamilySearch Catalog, collections, and digitized-volume searches all returned empty for this place/period; that likely reflects a search gap rather than a true absence of digitized material.

---

*This guide is grounded in what the FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont Genealogy page and this session's tool results actually state. Where a search came back empty or a detail was not addressed, it is flagged as a gap rather than filled from background knowledge. A research plan sequencing specific searches — starting with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule and individual town clerk records — can be built from this guide once you are ready.*

# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom. Yorkshire was historically one county (dateRange 866-1801 per place_search) and continues as a modern county grouping from 1801.
- **Administrative note:** By 1851 Yorkshire was long since divided for local administration into three Ridings - West, North, and East - which is how most record collections and finding aids file material.
- **Population:** place_population returned no data for this standardPlace in this survey; not established here.
- **Economy/Ethnic composition/Religious denominations:** Not established by tool results this run; West Yorkshire mill towns and the woollen/textile industry are reflected in the occupation, poor-law and workhouse record series found below.

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change is evidenced for the 1851 target year itself; Yorkshire's division into Ridings predates and persists through the period. Modern 1974 county reorganisation (splitting Yorkshire further) postdates the target period and is not relevant to 1851 records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** National civil registration of births, marriages and deaths in England and Wales is evidenced by FamilySearch collection 2285341 (England and Wales, Death Registration Index, 1837-2007) and the parallel Birth (1837-2008) and Marriage (1837-2005) Registration Indexes - all beginning 1837, at the national (England and Wales) level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched this run did not state this independently (see quirks).
- **What exists:** For 1851, the GRO Death Registration Index covers the target year; search it by name/quarter/year, then order the full GRO death certificate.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (national); indexed copy via FamilySearch and findmypast (https://www.findmypast.com/search/results?datasetname=england+%26+wales+deaths+1837-2007&sid=103&county=yorkshire).
- **Gaps:** Index gives name, age, registration district and quarter only - not cause of death or informant - the full certificate must be ordered from the GRO.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Parish burial registers (see Church records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England parish registers are the main pre-/post-1837 source; Non-Conformist (chapel) records are also catalogued separately for Yorkshire.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; West Yorkshire's Church of England Deaths and Burials collection runs 1813-1985 (Ancestry collection 2254) and North Yorkshire's equivalent runs 1813-1995 (Ancestry collection 62238) - both cover 1851.
- **Where held:** Parish chests / diocesan record offices; Bishop's Transcripts for Yorkshire (FamilySearch collection 4319956, 1547-1938, 11.85M people) and Yorkshire Parish Registers (FamilySearch collection 4439317, 1550-2006, 27.3M people) are both digitized and cover 1851.
- **Gaps:** Coverage is filed separately by Riding (West/North/East) in several external indexes - a search of only one riding's collection will miss a death recorded in another.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** England and Wales Census 1851 (FamilySearch collection 2563939, 1,569,726 people) - directly in the target year, useful to confirm the person was alive and resident shortly before an 1851 death, or to find the household for a death later in the year.
- **Access:** Indexed with images via FamilySearch; also on Ancestry and findmypast per external links.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills and administrations.
- **Where held:** Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858 (Ancestry collection 5246) covers 1851; from 1858 the England and Wales National Probate Calendar applies (FamilySearch collection 2451051, starts 1858, just after the target year). The Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York, is a named repository for Yorkshire ecclesiastical probate (http://www.york.ac.uk/borthwick/).
- **Testate or intestate:** Determines whether to search will indexes or administration grants - not established for this person; check both.

### Land records
- Not established by tool results this run for 1851 Yorkshire specifically; West Yorkshire Select Land Tax Records, 1704-1932 (Ancestry collection 5108) cover the period if land tax is relevant.

### Military records
- No conflict is active in England itself in 1851; not a priority record type for this death search.

### Cemetery records
- West Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials (as above) functions as the main burial index; no separate FindAGrave/BillionGraves coverage was identified by tool results this run.

### Newspaper records
- Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner (1851-1982) and Farmer's Friend and Freeman's Journal (1850-1855) both run through 1851 and are West/South Yorkshire-area papers per findmypast (https://www.findmypast.com/newspapers/england/huddersfield-and-holmfirth-examiner, https://www.findmypast.com/newspapers/england/farmers-friend-and-freemans-journal) - worth checking for a death/burial notice.
- **Where held:** findmypast newspaper archive (subscription).

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not a priority for a death within Yorkshire; omitted as inapplicable to this specific research question.

### Tax records
- West Yorkshire, England, Select Rate Books, Accounts and Censuses, 1705-1893 (Ancestry collection 9016, via https://search.ancestry.co.uk/search/db.aspx?dbid=9016) could substitute if the person is not found in the main indexes.

### Other record types
- West Yorkshire Poor Law and Township Records, 1663-1914 (Ancestry collection 9017) and Workhouse records may record a pauper's death where no family could register it.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

| FamilySearch | England and Wales Death Registration Index 1837-2007 (id 2285341); England and Wales Census 1851 (id 2563939); Yorkshire Bishop's Transcripts (id 4319956); Yorkshire Parish Registers (id 4439317); England Deaths and Burials 1538-1991 (id 1473016) | National GRO death index coverage and parish burial coverage for 1851 | Free |
| Ancestry | West Yorkshire Church of England Deaths and Burials 1813-1985 (collection 2254); North Yorkshire Church of England Deaths and Burials 1813-1995 (collection 62238); Yorkshire Probate Records 1521-1858 (collection 5246) | Riding-specific burial coverage; pre-1858 probate | Subscription |
| findmypast | England & Wales Deaths 1837-2007 (county=yorkshire search); Yorkshire Burials; Yorkshire newspaper titles (Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner, etc.) | GRO index cross-search; local newspaper death notices | Subscription |
| FreeBMD | FreeBMD Search (https://www.freebmd.org.uk/search) | Free alternative GRO birth/marriage/death index search | Free |
| Yorkshire BMD | Yorkshire Births Marriages & Deaths Indexes (http://www.yorkshirebmd.org.uk/) | Volunteer-run regional BMD index, may supplement GRO index | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York | Yorkshire ecclesiastical probate and parish records | In-person / written request (http://www.york.ac.uk/borthwick/) |
| General Register Office | Original 1851 death registration and certificate | Certificate order by post/online |
| Explore York Archives and Local History | Local Yorkshire archival holdings | In-person (https://exploreyork.org.uk/archives/) |

## Records NOT online
- Full GRO death certificates themselves are not available online in image form; only the index is online, and the certificate must be ordered from the GRO.
- Original parish registers not yet digitized by the collections above remain physical-only at local record offices.

## Known record losses
- No record loss for this place/period was stated by any tool result in this survey; none is claimed.

## Research tips
- Search the GRO Death Registration Index (FamilySearch collection 2285341, or findmypast's county=yorkshire death search) by surname and approximate year/quarter, since civil registration was in force nationally from 1837.
- Cross-check against the Riding-specific Church of England burial collections (West Yorkshire collection 2254, North Yorkshire collection 62238) - the family may appear in parish burial records even if the civil index entry is misindexed.
- Use the 1851 Census (FamilySearch collection 2563939) to confirm the person's last known household and residence, narrowing which registration district's death index to search.
- Check FreeBMD and Yorkshire BMD as free cross-checks against the subscription indexes.
- Consult local newspapers (e.g. Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner, 1851-1982) for a death or burial notice.
- If the death cannot be found under the expected surname, search neighbouring Ridings' collections too, since Yorkshire sources are split by Riding rather than filed under one county-wide index.

# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom. Yorkshire was historically one county (dateRange 866-1801 per place_search) and continues as a modern county grouping from 1801.
- **Administrative note:** By 1851 Yorkshire was long since divided for local administration into three Ridings - West, North, and East - which is how most record collections and finding aids file material.
- **Population:** place_population returned no data for this standardPlace in this survey; not established here.
- **Economy/Ethnic composition/Religious denominations:** Not established by tool results this run; West Yorkshire mill towns and the woollen/textile industry are reflected in the occupation, poor-law and workhouse record series found below.

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change is evidenced for the 1851 target year itself; Yorkshire's division into Ridings predates and persists through the period. Modern 1974 county reorganisation (splitting Yorkshire further) postdates the target period and is not relevant to 1851 records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** National civil registration of births, marriages and deaths in England and Wales is evidenced by FamilySearch collection 2285341 (England and Wales, Death Registration Index, 1837-2007) and the parallel Birth (1837-2008) and Marriage (1837-2005) Registration Indexes - all beginning 1837, at the national (England and Wales) level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched this run did not state this independently (see quirks).
- **What exists:** For 1851, the GRO Death Registration Index covers the target year; search it by name/quarter/year, then order the full GRO death certificate.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (national); indexed copy via FamilySearch and findmypast (https://www.findmypast.com/search/results?datasetname=england+%26+wales+deaths+1837-2007&sid=103&county=yorkshire).
- **Gaps:** Index gives name, age, registration district and quarter only - not cause of death or informant - the full certificate must be ordered from the GRO.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Parish burial registers (see Church records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England parish registers are the main pre-/post-1837 source; Non-Conformist (chapel) records are also catalogued separately for Yorkshire.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; West Yorkshire's Church of England Deaths and Burials collection runs 1813-1985 (Ancestry collection 2254) and North Yorkshire's equivalent runs 1813-1995 (Ancestry collection 62238) - both cover 1851.
- **Where held:** Parish chests / diocesan record offices; Bishop's Transcripts for Yorkshire (FamilySearch collection 4319956, 1547-1938, 11.85M people) and Yorkshire Parish Registers (FamilySearch collection 4439317, 1550-2006, 27.3M people) are both digitized and cover 1851.
- **Gaps:** Coverage is filed separately by Riding (West/North/East) in several external indexes - a search of only one riding's collection will miss a death recorded in another.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** England and Wales Census 1851 (FamilySearch collection 2563939, 1,569,726 people) - directly in the target year, useful to confirm the person was alive and resident shortly before an 1851 death, or to find the household for a death later in the year.
- **Access:** Indexed with images via FamilySearch; also on Ancestry and findmypast per external links.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills and administrations.
- **Where held:** Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858 (Ancestry collection 5246) covers 1851; from 1858 the England and Wales National Probate Calendar applies (FamilySearch collection 2451051, starts 1858, just after the target year). The Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York, is a named repository for Yorkshire ecclesiastical probate (http://www.york.ac.uk/borthwick/).
- **Testate or intestate:** Determines whether to search will indexes or administration grants - not established for this person; check both.

### Land records
- Not established by tool results this run for 1851 Yorkshire specifically; West Yorkshire Select Land Tax Records, 1704-1932 (Ancestry collection 5108) cover the period if land tax is relevant.

### Military records
- No conflict is active in England itself in 1851; not a priority record type for this death search.

### Cemetery records
- West Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials (as above) functions as the main burial index; no separate FindAGrave/BillionGraves coverage was identified by tool results this run.

### Newspaper records
- Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner (1851-1982) and Farmer's Friend and Freeman's Journal (1850-1855) both run through 1851 and are West/South Yorkshire-area papers per findmypast (https://www.findmypast.com/newspapers/england/huddersfield-and-holmfirth-examiner, https://www.findmypast.com/newspapers/england/farmers-friend-and-freemans-journal) - worth checking for a death/burial notice.
- **Where held:** findmypast newspaper archive (subscription).

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not a priority for a death within Yorkshire; omitted as inapplicable to this specific research question.

### Tax records
- West Yorkshire, England, Select Rate Books, Accounts and Censuses, 1705-1893 (Ancestry collection 9016, via https://search.ancestry.co.uk/search/db.aspx?dbid=9016) could substitute if the person is not found in the main indexes.

### Other record types
- West Yorkshire Poor Law and Township Records, 1663-1914 (Ancestry collection 9017) and Workhouse records may record a pauper's death where no family could register it.
